title: Threat Actor Attribution
summary: Threat actor attribution is the analytical practice of linking an intrusion or campaign to a specific group, and sometimes to a sponsor or state, by correlating technical artefacts with behaviour, infrastructure, targeting and language clues. It relies on the overlap of many independent observations rather than a single indicator, because tools, malware families and infrastructure are shared, rented, resold or deliberately imitated by other groups. In real environments attribution appears in intelligence reporting, sanctions and legal decisions, and incident briefings, where it shapes how aggressively a victim responds, how much leadership attention the case receives, and which future threats are monitored. The mistake readers and junior analysts make is treating attribution as proven fact: careful public statements are graded with confidence levels and rest on multiple sources, while early low confidence assessments are often repeated later as certainty. A second error is letting attribution drive defensive priorities, since most protective action does not depend on knowing who the intruder is.

beginner.definition: Threat actor attribution means deciding which group carried out an attack. A threat actor is a person or a group that attacks computer systems. Attribution is the work of linking an attack to a known group. Analysts compare many clues instead of trusting one.
beginner.whyItMatters: Knowing who attacked you can change how you respond and who you tell. It helps leaders judge whether an incident looks like a crime, an espionage attempt or a protest. It also guides which threats you watch for next. However, a confident guess can cause serious harm, such as blaming the wrong country. Teams must state how sure they are and explain the evidence behind the claim.
howItWorks: Analysts collect technical clues such as file names, tools and network addresses used in the attack.
They compare those clues with reports about groups that other researchers have already described.
They study behaviour, including which systems were targeted and which files were taken.
They look at timing, language settings and working hours for extra hints.
They weigh how easily each clue could be copied or faked by a different group.
They publish a judgement with a stated level of confidence and the reasons behind it.
beginner.example: Imagine a night watchman investigating a broken window at a warehouse. He finds a scratched mark, a muddy boot print and a note in a language used by a nearby crew. Each clue alone means little, because anyone can copy a mark or a boot. Together with the timing and the tools left behind, they build a story he can defend. Threat actor attribution works the same way, and a careful watchman says how sure he is.
takeaways: Attribution links an attack to a group by combining many clues, not one indicator.
Always state a confidence level, because clues can be copied or shared between groups.
Defensive action usually does not depend on naming the attacker.

objectives: Explain what threat actor attribution is and what it tries to establish.
Describe the types of evidence analysts correlate before naming a group.
Explain why indicators can be shared, rented or deliberately imitated.
Describe how confidence levels are used when reporting attribution.
Explain why attribution should not drive defensive priorities.
Identify the risks of publishing an attribution judgement too early.
